title: Adaptive flow control and cross-language compatibility for SDK streaming & pagination
creator: Aisha Park
description: PRD to define cross-language SDK requirements for adaptive flow control, resumable pagination, robust retry semantics, and streaming compatibility across Python/TypeScript/Go clients. Deliverables: concrete API surface, acceptance tests, migration guidance, and rollout plan for backwards-compatible rollout in sdk-2026.04.
background: Multiple customers have built streaming and paginated integrations and reported divergent behaviors between our Python and TypeScript SDKs: cursor semantics differ, streaming reconnection logic is ad-hoc, and retry policies produce surprising duplicate side-effects. Engineering has proposed runtime work on server-side resume tokens and adaptive batching. This PRD aligns client contract changes across languages and minimizes breaking surface area.
scope: Define and deliver: 1) unified paginated iterator contract (cursor encoding, resume semantics); 2) streaming API with reconnect/resume hooks and backpressure guidance; 3) standard retry/backoff policy and idempotency guidance; 4) compatibility matrix and deprecation policy for old helpers. Deliver language-specific reference implementations and e2e tests.
out_of_scope: Changes to server response formats beyond adding an opaque resume_token (no new top-level fields), persistent storage semantics for customer data, and deep refactors of internal SDK packaging/monorepo layouts.
requirements: PaginatedIterator: sync and async variants where applicable; supports next()/hasNext() and async iterator protocols in each language
Server returns opaque resume_token string; clients must treat as opaque and persist it verbatim in cursors
Cursor format at client level: base64-encoded JSON blob containing resume_token and client-side position metadata; server ignores client metadata
Resume semantics: next() after a resumed cursor must continue from the first item NOT previously delivered to caller; duplication must be avoided for primary flows

Streaming API: support chunked chunk+meta framing and event-based (SSE/WebSocket) transport; provide on_open, on_message, on_error, on_close callbacks and a resumable reconnect strategy using last_event_id
Adaptive flow control: client should expose a knob for max_inflight_messages and implement slow-consumer backpressure mitigation (pause/resume consumption, automatic holdoff with exponential backoff)

Retries: default retry policy = jittered exponential backoff with base 200ms, factor 2, max 60s, max attempts 7 for idempotent reads; non-idempotent writes require idempotency_key header or be single-attempt by default
Compatibility: new surface must be additive; any breaking or opt-in changes must use minor version bumps and explicit migration docs
Logging/Observability: SDK emits structured telemetry events for reconnect attempts, resume token usage, retry counts, and unrecoverable failures
Tests: language-specific e2e where client talks to a test harness simulating partial streams, cursor rotation, and server-side token invalidation
acceptance_criteria: All three SDKs (Python, TS, Go) provide a PaginatedIterator implementation matching the contract in requirements and pass the cross-language resume test suite
Streaming client implements reconnect-and-resume with last_event_id and passes simulated network partition scenarios in e2e tests
Default retry/backoff behavior is implemented consistently and documented; a non-default policy override hook is available in all SDKs
Compatibility policy documented: deprecation window of at least 90 days for removed helpers, and a migration guide published in docs.redwood.ai
Telemetry: reconnects, retries, resume token usage surface in Console or an exported debug stream for at least 30 days in internal tests
Benchmarks: no more than 10% increase in median latency for a typical paginated fetch path after adding cursor wrapping
API signatures for examples are reviewed and approved by SDK owners and PM
api_examples:
Python sync iterator example: for page in client.list_items_paged(resource='widget'):
    	for item in page.items:
    		process(item)
    	# resume: saved_cursor = page.cursor
    	# client.resume_from_cursor(saved_cursor)
TypeScript async iterator example: for await (const item of client.listItemsPaged({ resource: 'widget' })) { process(item); } // exposes .resume(cursor) on returned iterator
Go example: it := client.ListItemsPaged(ctx, ListOptions{Resource:'widget'}); for it.Next() { item := it.Item(); process(item) } // it.Cursor() returns opaque string for resume
compatibility_rules: Opaque resume_token from server MUST be forwarded unchanged by clients; clients may wrap it for storage but server token must be included in resume requests
Clients MUST not infer internal server semantics from token contents; tokens are opaque and may rotate
Additive helpers: any new convenience helpers are shipped in minor releases and documented with equivalence to primitive APIs
Removal policy: announce deprecations via console dashboard + SDK changelog, provide migration snippets, and allow both old and new helpers to coexist for 90 days
Semver guidance: feature additions -> minor bump, breaking changes -> major bump and opt-in flags for a transition period
migration_plan: Phase 1 (2 weeks): land server resume_token endpoint and spec; Phase 2 (3 weeks): implement PaginatedIterator in all SDKs behind feature flag; Phase 3 (2 weeks): e2e tests and performance validation; Phase 4 (2 weeks): documentation, migration guides, and staged rollout to beta customers; Phase 5: general availability in sdk-2026.04. Customers on older SDKs continue to work; we will not block on client upgrades.
rollout_plan: Alpha: SDK owners and 3 internal Redwood teams test feature-flagged clients (1 week)
Beta: invite 5 customers with streaming/pagination usage to opt in and provide feedback (2 weeks)
GA: remove feature flag after 90 days if no regressions discovered; make migration notes prominent in changelog
qa_tests: Cross-language resume suite: simulate partial page returns and verify no duplicates or missing items after resume
Streaming reconnection suite: network drop mid-stream, then reconnect and resume from last_event_id; verify ordering and at-least-once vs exactly-once tradeoffs documented
Fuzz cursor corruption: ensure SDK surfaces clear errors and provides actionable messages when server rejects tokens
Load testing: measure 99th percentile latency with default client settings and with adaptive flow control enabled
Idempotency tests: non-idempotent endpoints must reject duplicate requests when no idempotency_key provided; clients must expose idempotency helper
decision_log: 2026-02-20: Decided to use opaque resume_token provided by server instead of client-managed offsets to allow backend re-sharding without client changes
2026-02-27: Chose jittered exponential backoff defaults (base=200ms, factor=2, max=60s, attempts=7) after load modeling; override hooks required
2026-03-03: Streaming API will expose both chunk/frame semantics and event-based handlers to accommodate different transport layers and language idioms
2026-03-10: Compatibility policy set to 90-day coexistence for removed helpers and additive-only approach for initial release
notes: Trade-offs: exactly-once semantics are not practical across network partitions; default behavior will be at-least-once with guidance for deduplication via ids in payloads
Performance: wrapping resume_token in base64 client-side adds ~32 bytes per cursor; negligible compared to typical payloads but measured in benchmarks
Telemetry: lightweight counters preferred over verbose traces by default to avoid telemetry costs for customers
